displayQuote: To be popular is easy; to be right, when right is unpopular, is noble

meta.title: Who really said "To be popular is easy; to be right, when right is unpopular, is noble"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Andrew Carnegie said it at a Lotos Club dinner on 27 Jan 1900 — but every paper that reported him ends the sentence “is difficult,” not “is noble.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To be popular is easy; to be right, when right is unpopular, is noble'?
meta.ogDescription: The real 1900 wording ends “is difficult.” Quotle.info traces the line to Carnegie's Lotos Club speech and the newspapers that carried it.

answer.label: Not quite Carnegie — he said “is difficult,” not “is noble”
answer.sourceLine: Carnegie really did say a sentence almost exactly like this — at a dinner given in his honour by the Lotos Club in New York on 27 January 1900, in the middle of a passage attacking war fever and the slogan “our country, right or wrong.” But the three newspapers that carried the wire report the next morning all end it the same way: “to be right when right is unpopular is difficult.” The circulating version swaps the last word for noble, which turns a rueful admission into a compliment.

source.excerpt: As for money given to beggars of whose needs and habits we are ignorant, I can conceive of no use of money so well calculated to increase pauperism and demoralize the people. To be popular is easy; to be right when right is unpopular is difficult. When the passions are aroused and the war fever rages any man can be popular who howls for war, but the most valuable citizen of the State at that time will probably be the citizen who opposes the drawing of the sword.
trail: Carnegie was guest of honour at a Lotos Club dinner in New York on the evening of 27 January 1900. The wire report of his remarks ran the next morning in The San Francisco Call ↗, which prints: “To be popular is easy; to be right when right is unpopular is difficult.”

The identical wire text appears the same day on page 7 of The Indianapolis Journal ↗ under “Carnegie’s Philosophy”, and on the front page of The Seattle Post-Intelligencer ↗. All three end the sentence “is difficult”; a phrase search of the same archive for the “is noble” form returns nothing.

The Lotos Club printed its own text of the speech a year later in Speeches at the Lotos Club ↗ (pp. 351–56). That version is shorter and tidier, and the sentence is not in it — nor is the “our country, right or wrong” passage that surrounds it in the press reports.
The wording that circulates today comes down a much thinner line: Wikiquote ↗ lists it under Undated, citing a 2002 article in The Nation ↗, which gives the “noble” form with no source of its own.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the Library of Congress’s OCR of the Call’s page, with obvious scanning slips corrected. The Indianapolis Journal breaks the line into two sentences (“To be popular is easy. To be right when right is unpopular is difficult.”); the Seattle Post-Intelligencer punctuates it exactly as the modern misquote does — “to be popular is easy; to be right, when right is unpopular, is difficult” — which is how far the corruption really extends: one word.

author.name: Andrew Carnegie
author.heading: Andrew Carnegie
author.bio: Born in Dunfermline, Scotland, Carnegie built the largest steel business in the United States and then spent the rest of his life giving the proceeds away — most famously in free public libraries. He was also, by 1900, one of the loudest American opponents of the annexation of the Philippines, which is the argument he was in the middle of when he said this. The Lotos Club dinner speech shows both halves of him at once: an unsentimental lecture on why indiscriminate charity breeds pauperism, followed by a flat refusal to say my country, right or wrong.

misattribution.heading: Where it goes wrong
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake quote. It is a real Carnegie sentence with its last word replaced — and, in most retellings, with the wrong occasion attached or none at all.

items.why: Every contemporaneous report ends the sentence “is difficult.” The word noble does turn up three sentences later in the same passage — “It should be the symbol of what is right, noble and just” — in the report in The San Francisco Call ↗, so a bleed from one line to the other is a plausible route, though nothing documents the swap.

items.who: A June 1885 talk to Pittsburgh business students
items.why: The line is sometimes pinned to Carnegie’s 1885 address The Road to Business Success. The text of that address ↗ contains neither “popular is easy” nor the word “unpopular” anywhere in it — and neither does the book it was later collected in.
Wikiquote ↗ files the “noble” version under Undated, its sole citation a 2002 piece in The Nation ↗ — which quotes it with no date, no occasion and no source.

misattribution.truthLine: He did say it, on 27 January 1900, at a Lotos Club dinner in his own honour — and he said difficult: “To be popular is easy; to be right when right is unpopular is difficult” ↗.

context.heading: What he was actually arguing about
lead: This is not a business maxim, though it is usually sold as one. Carnegie said it while explaining, to a room of admirers, why he had spent the previous eighteen months making himself unpopular over the Philippines. The San Francisco Call ran the report under the subhead “Turning to National Policy, the Millionaire Justifies His Course in Striving Against Imperialism”; the Seattle Post-Intelligencer put it on the front page as “Carnegie Talks Again.”

The sentence is the hinge of the passage, and the sentences on either side of it make the meaning unmissable: “When the passions are aroused and the war fever rages any man can be popular who howls for war, but the most valuable citizen of the State at that time will probably be the citizen who opposes the drawing of the sword.” Then: “I repudiate with scorn the immoral doctrine, our country, right or wrong.” Read in place, “difficult” is the honest word. “Noble” is the word a poster wants.
context.detailsSummary: Why the Lotos Club’s own book doesn’t contain the line
detailsBody: The Club published its after-dinner speeches in 1901, and Carnegie’s 27 January 1900 remarks are there at pages 351–56. That text is noticeably shorter and smoother than the wire report, and it has no “popular is easy” sentence at all — the nearest thing is “This may seem harsh doctrine, perhaps not popular; but I am not concerned about popularity; I know I am right.” The whole passage on war fever and “our country, right or wrong” is absent too.

There is a nice irony in that, because in the very same speech Carnegie complains about exactly this problem. Describing an earlier address of his, he says the reporter present “took a few of the more striking words of my address, and I scarcely recognized myself in print the next day,” and adds: “Public speakers have to beware of the epigrammatic.” The epigram the reporters kept that night is the one still in circulation — only they kept it more accurately than the internet has.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Library of Congress issue of The San Francisco Call for 28 January 1900; its page 16 report of the Lotos Club dinner contains “To be popular is easy; to be right when right is unpopular is difficult.” (confirmed by reading the Library of Congress OCR for that page)

The Library of Congress issue of The Indianapolis Journal for 28 January 1900; page 7 (Part One) carries the same wire report under “Carnegie’s Philosophy”, rendering the line as two sentences ending “is difficult” (confirmed by reading the Library of Congress OCR for that page)

The Library of Congress issue of The Seattle Post-Intelligencer for 28 January 1900; the front page carries “Carnegie Talks Again”, giving “to be popular is easy; to be right, when right is unpopular, is difficult” (confirmed by reading the Library of Congress OCR for that page)

Speeches at the Lotos Club (New York: privately printed, 1901), arranged by John Elderkin, Chester S. Lord and Horatio N. Fraser, prints Carnegie’s speech “at the dinner in his honor, January 27, 1900” at pp. 351–56, and that text contains no occurrence of the word “unpopular”

Wikiquote’s Andrew Carnegie page lists “To be popular is easy; to be right when right is unpopular, is noble…” under its Undated heading, cited only to “An Imperial Moment” (5 December 2002) in The Nation

The Nation’s “An Imperial Moment” quotes Carnegie as “To be popular is easy; to be right when right is unpopular, is noble… I repudiate with scorn the immoral doctrine, ‘Our country, right or wrong’”, giving no date or source for the words
The full text of Carnegie’s 1885 address “The Road to Business Success” contains neither “to be popular is easy” nor “right is unpopular”
Carnegie’s Autobiography contains no occurrence of the sentence; its only use of “unpopular” is an unrelated remark about McKinley and withdrawal from the Philippines

The Gospel of Wealth and Other Timely Essays — the volume collecting Carnegie’s anti-imperialist essays “Distant Possessions” and “Americanism versus Imperialism” — contains no occurrence of “unpopular” and not this sentence
The Empire of Business, which reprints “The Road to Business Success: A Talk to Young Men”, contains no occurrence of the word “unpopular”
